Constants

DONOTCACHEPAGE

crawl-guard.php : 318
public mixed DONOTCACHEPAGE = true

DONOTMINIFY

fragment-response.php : 444
public mixed DONOTMINIFY = \true

JPKCOM_POSTFILTER_ABILITY_CATEGORY

abilities.php : 23

Ability category shared with the other JPKCom content plugins.

public mixed JPKCOM_POSTFILTER_ABILITY_CATEGORY = 'jpkcom-content'

JPKCOM_POSTFILTER_ABILITY_INPUT_KEYS

abilities.php : 60

Input keys each ability accepts at the top level.

public mixed JPKCOM_POSTFILTER_ABILITY_INPUT_KEYS = ['jpkcom-post-filter/list-filters' => ['post_type'], 'jpkcom-post-filter/query-posts' => ['post_type', 'filters', 'page', 'per_page', 'search']]

Neither input schema declares additionalProperties, so core drops an unknown key before the callback ever sees it. Without this list a caller that flattens the nested map - category instead of filters.category, the commonest shape error a tool-calling model makes - is answered with the complete unfiltered corpus, HTTP 200 and filters: }, which reads like a successful filtered query. That is the failure jpkcom_postfilter_ability_validate_filters() exists to prevent, reached by a route that guard does not stand on.

JPKCOM_POSTFILTER_ABILITY_PER_PAGE_DEFAULT

abilities.php : 28

Default page size for the query ability.

public mixed JPKCOM_POSTFILTER_ABILITY_PER_PAGE_DEFAULT = 10

JPKCOM_POSTFILTER_ABILITY_PER_PAGE_MAX

abilities.php : 33

Maximum page size for the query ability.

public mixed JPKCOM_POSTFILTER_ABILITY_PER_PAGE_MAX = 50

JPKCOM_POSTFILTER_ABILITY_SEARCH_MAX_BYTES

abilities.php : 47

Longest search term, in BYTES, that WP_Query will actually apply.

public mixed JPKCOM_POSTFILTER_ABILITY_SEARCH_MAX_BYTES = 1600

WP_Query::parse_query() blanks s when strlen() exceeds this, as an anti-DoS measure, and it does so silently: no error, no filter, no notice. Because that happens inside the query, past every check an ability could make, the caller receives exactly the answer it would have got with no search term at all.

The unit is bytes, not characters, because core calls strlen() rather than mb_strlen() - so 801 x U+00FC is over the limit at 801 characters. A maxLength in the JSON Schema counts characters and would therefore leave the hole open.

JPKCOM_POSTFILTER_CACHE_GROUP

cache-manager.php : 30

Cache group used for wp_cache_* calls.

public mixed JPKCOM_POSTFILTER_CACHE_GROUP = 'jpkcom_postfilter'

JPKCOM_POSTFILTER_CACHE_TTL

Default TTL for transient-based caches (seconds).

public string JPKCOM_POSTFILTER_FRAGMENT_ERROR_STRIPPED = '<div data-jpkpf-fragment-error="markers-stripped"></div>'

JPKCOM_POSTFILTER_ZONE_END

fragment-response.php : 70

Marker written immediately after a swappable zone

public string JPKCOM_POSTFILTER_ZONE_END = '<template data-jpkpf-zone="end"></template>'
Tags
since
1.2.0
1.4.4

An element instead of an HTML comment.

JPKCOM_POSTFILTER_ZONE_START

fragment-response.php : 61

Marker written immediately before a swappable zone

public string JPKCOM_POSTFILTER_ZONE_START = '<template data-jpkpf-zone="start"></template>'

An empty <template> and not an HTML comment, since 1.4.4. Comments are precisely what an HTML minifier is built to delete: Autoptimize ships with "Optimize HTML Code" on and "Keep HTML comments" off, and its buffer is the inner one (template_redirect priority 2 against this file's 0), so it minified the page before jpkcom_postfilter_extract_zones() ever saw it. Both markers gone, no zone found, a 0-byte 200 on every filter click. Measured on the verification install: 18 300 B with Autoptimize off, 0 B with its stock settings, 18 300 B again with autoptimize_html off and 8 976 B with autoptimize_html_keepcomments on — which isolates it to the comment stripping and nothing else about Autoptimize.

No minifier removes elements, so a marker that is an element survives all of them; <template> because it renders nothing and is valid almost anywhere, including inside a table. It never reaches a browser either way — extraction returns what lies between the markers.

Tags
since
1.2.0
1.4.4

An element instead of an HTML comment.

A configured group whose taxonomy is not registered is skipped. The configuration outlives the registration - deactivating the plugin that registered a taxonomy leaves its filter group behind - and a group in that state would otherwise be reported as filterable while jpkcom_postfilter_build_tax_query() drops the clause it produces (query-handler.php:57), which is the silent-full-corpus failure the validation guard exists to prevent. Skipping the group here turns that case into a jpkcom_postfilter_unknown_taxonomy error that names the real ones.

This is why the function reads WordPress state; it is not pure.

jpkcom_postfilter_ability_validate_filters()

abilities.php : 264

Reject filters that name a taxonomy which is not filterable

jpkcom_postfilter_ability_validate_filters(array<string, array<string|int, string>> $filters, array<string|int, string> $allowed_taxonomies) : true|WP_Error

The query pipeline drops an unknown taxonomy clause silently and then returns the complete unfiltered result set, so this check is the only thing standing between a mistyped taxonomy and a wrong answer presented as a filtered one. The error message names the valid taxonomies so the caller can correct itself without another round trip.

Carries data['status'] = 400. The REST run controller returns the WP_Error verbatim and rest_ensure_response() defaults to 500 without it - which tells an agent "transient server fault, retry the same call", the exact opposite of the self-correction this message is written for.

jpkcom_postfilter_ability_excerpt()

abilities.php : 655

Read a post's excerpt without letting the embed handler write to the database

jpkcom_postfilter_ability_excerpt(WP_Post $post) : string

get_the_excerpt() on a post with an empty post_excerpt runs wp_trim_excerpt(), which applies the whole the_content chain. WP_Embed registers TWO callbacks on that chain at priority 8 - run_shortcode (class-wp-embed.php:33) and autoembed (:41) - and both end up in WP_Embed::shortcode().

In an ability callback there is no post context, so that method takes the branch at class-wp-embed.php:317-366 rather than the update_post_meta one: it fetches the URL over the network and calls wp_insert_post() with post_type => 'oembed_cache' and post_status => 'publish'. Measured on WP 7.0.3 against 1.3.0: a GET to a route annotated readonly: true wrote a published post authored by the calling subscriber, and made one outbound request per URL - 3.5 s cold for three of them. Any user with read can trigger it.

Both callbacks are removed for the duration of the read and put back afterwards, and nothing else in the chain is touched, so the delivered string is byte-identical to what 1.3.0 returned. That is the whole reason this shape was chosen over projecting the excerpt from raw content: a raw projection changes 10 of 17 measured content shapes and has to reimplement the password gate, the <!--more--> and <!--nextpage--> cuts and the block allow-list, which is core's own function copied into a plugin and going stale on every release.

KNOWN LIMIT, on purpose: this closes the case, not the class. do_shortcode still runs at priority 11, and every other the_content callback still runs. A registered shortcode that writes would write here too. The general rule - an ability callback has no post context, so no accessor whose contract is "as the front end would render it" may be called - is documented in CLAUDE.md, and get_permalink(), get_the_terms() and list-filters' get_terms() are in the same class and have not been audited.

Parameters
$post : WP_Post

Post to read.

Tags
since
1.3.1
Return values
string —

The excerpt, exactly as get_the_excerpt() produces it.

Decide whether a filter set survives a round trip through a filter URL

Above the caps a built URL does not show the result set the ability just reported: until 1.5.0 the parser truncated it to the first slugs (measured with four category slugs against max_filters_per_group = 3, where the link resolved to the first three), since 1.5.0 the request guard rejects it with 404/410.

Until 1.5.0 this function was a hand-maintained copy of the parser's truncation rule, and nothing noticed when the two drifted. It now asks the one function the parser, the request guard and the term links ask.

jpkcom_postfilter_apcu_key()

cache-manager.php : 56

APCu key for a plugin cache key, scoped to this site

jpkcom_postfilter_apcu_key(string $key) : string

APCu is one memory segment per PHP-FPM pool, shared by every WordPress install the pool serves and by every site of a multisite network. Until 1.5.0 the key was jpkpf_ + an MD5 of the query arguments only, so two sites running the same filter query read each other's cached WP_Query - one site's posts on another site's page. The WordPress object cache does not have this problem: it prefixes per blog itself.

Parameters
$key : string

Plugin cache key ('' for the bare prefix).

Tags
since
1.5.0
Return values
string

jpkcom_postfilter_robots_txt_rules()

crawl-guard.php : 762

robots.txt rules for the filter URLs

jpkcom_postfilter_robots_txt_rules() : array<string|int, string>

Applies to every user agent alike - no crawler is locked out of content or of the single-term pages, only out of the combinations.

  • deep (default), with seo_index_max_terms = 1: {base}/{endpoint}/*+ any segment with more than one term Not *\/*\/ (proposed in the original analysis): it would also block _/term/ - the single-term pages of the second group, which the default link mode links to and which are indexable - and the pagination of every single-term page. Blocked but linked pages end up "indexed, though blocked by robots.txt". Two-segment combinations are not linked in single mode and are noindex anyway.
  • all: the whole endpoint
  • off: nothing

With seo_index_max_terms = 0 "deep" becomes "all"; with 2 or more the indexable pages cannot be told apart by a wildcard, so only the fragment and query-var lines are emitted.

Tags
since
1.5.0
Return values
array<string|int, string> —

Lines without the User-agent line.

jpkcom_postfilter_term_href()

crawl-guard.php : 866

Where a term button links to - or null for no link at all

jpkcom_postfilter_term_href(string $base_url, array<string, array<string|int, string>> $active_filters, string $taxonomy, string $slug, bool $is_active) : string|null

The script never reads these hrefs: it intercepts every click and builds the URL from the button states. The hrefs serve clients without JavaScript, which in practice means crawlers. They are therefore the generator of the URL space a crawler can discover, and the link mode decides its size:

  • single (default): an inactive term links to its own single-term page, an active term to the selection without it while at most one term is left. Crawlable: the archive plus one page per term.
  • combo: "current selection ± this term", as before 1.5.0, but never beyond the caps, never deeper than JPKCOM_POSTFILTER_LINK_MAX_TERMS, and on an empty result page not into another group (that can only narrow nothing further).
  • none: no hrefs, buttons only.

jpkcom_postfilter_htaccess_parse()

htaccess-manager.php : 113

Split .htaccess content into lines and find the markers

jpkcom_postfilter_htaccess_parse(string $content) : array{bom: string, eol: string, lines: string[], blocks: array, damaged: bool, manual: bool, wp: ?int, misplaced: bool}

Each line keeps its own terminator (\n, \r\n or none for a last line without newline), so joining them gives back the exact bytes. Markers are compared as whole lines, ignoring surrounding blanks.

damaged means managed markers that do not pair up (BEGIN without END, END without BEGIN, BEGIN inside a block), or a managed block that holds one of WordPress's own marker lines (it spans or overlaps WordPress's block): where the block ends is then a guess - or replacing it would take WordPress's rewrite rules with it - and write and remove refuse.

misplaced means the first managed block sits below # BEGIN WordPress, where it never takes effect.

Parameters
$content : string

File content.

Tags
since
1.6.0
Return values

hash comes from the # rule <hash> line of the managed block, so a caller can compare it with the current rule hash. Beyond the interface of the plan: damaged (managed markers that do not pair up - write and remove refuse, and the admin page can say why) and misplaced (the managed block sits below WordPress's and never takes effect; the next write moves it, ruling R15).

For a write that shrinks the file: the new content is written over the old one first and the rest is cut afterwards, so for that instant the old tail would follow the new content - possibly half a directive, and Apache answers 500 for a .htaccess it cannot parse. Padded to the old length with # lines (at most 80 bytes each), every state of the file in between is the new content plus comments. Content that does not end with a newline gets one first, so the padding starts on its own line.

jpkcom_postfilter_htaccess_home_file()

htaccess-manager.php : 523

Path of the site's .htaccess as WordPress derives it: get_home_path()

jpkcom_postfilter_htaccess_home_file() : string

get_home_path() reads SCRIPT_FILENAME when home and siteurl differ (WordPress in a subdirectory). That is the PHP script of the request: the wp binary under WP-CLI, the root index.php on a front-end request - and from there the home path came out as '/' and the file as '/.htaccess'. So SCRIPT_FILENAME is ABSPATH for the call, which is what get_home_path() expects to find it below (WP-CLI's own rewrite command does the same); on an admin request the result is unchanged. When even that yields no home path (home and siteurl on different hosts), the WordPress directory is taken - never the file system root.

jpkcom_postfilter_htaccess_file()

htaccess-manager.php : 573

The path stored at Set up (option jpkcom_postfilter_htaccess_managed, fix wave item 1) while that file exists - a WP-CLI command, a cron run or a deactivation then works on the file the admin set up, whatever the request looks like. Otherwise (not set up, the legacy value '1', or the site moved and the stored file is gone) jpkcom_postfilter_htaccess_home_file().

The stored path is only trusted when its directory is one of the site's own: the WordPress directory, its parent (WordPress in a subdirectory) or the derived home path. A tampered option must not point the writes at another .htaccess on the host, and a subdirectory such as wp-content/uploads is never the right file either.

jpkcom_postfilter_htaccess_available()

htaccess-manager.php : 621

May the plugin manage the .htaccess on this site?

jpkcom_postfilter_htaccess_available() : array{ok: bool, reason: string}

Reasons, in the order they are checked:

  • litespeed: LiteSpeed reports itself as such, and WordPress's $is_apache is true for it too; OpenLiteSpeed also needs a restart to read .htaccess changes, so the plugin does not manage it there.
  • not-apache: SERVER_SOFTWARE does not name Apache (nginx, Caddy, FrankenPHP, Ferron, IIS, none).
  • multisite: one .htaccess serves the whole network.
  • file-mods-disallowed: DISALLOW_FILE_MODS is set.
  • no-file, not-writable: jpkcom_postfilter_htaccess_file().
  • manual-block: a pasted block with the manual markers is present; a second, managed one would apply the same rules twice.

The capability and nonce checks belong to the admin action.

Tags
since
1.6.0
Return values
array{ok: bool, reason: string}

Writing a looser block, like removing one, is always safe, so it is attempted whenever the file holds a managed block and is writable - whatever jpkcom_postfilter_htaccess_available() says and whatever SERVER_SOFTWARE names (empty under WP-CLI). Where the plugin may manage the file, a missing block is written, too.

False, with a reason, when a managed block (or markers that no longer pair up) stays stricter on a server that may read it (ruling R22).

jpkcom_postfilter_server_check_classify()

server-rules-check.php : 248

Turn the probe answers into a status

jpkcom_postfilter_server_check_classify(array<string, mixed> $responses, array<string, mixed> $inputs, string $server_software[, bool $robots_expected = true ]) : array{robots: string, rule: string, stricter: bool, stricter_checked: bool, stricter_suspected: bool, detail: string}

robots: ok when the body carries the plugin's fragment line (/*jpkpf-fragment), disabled when the plugin writes no robots.txt lines on this site, not-wordpress when something else answers robots.txt (a physical file, the web server), unreachable when the request did not get through.

rule (the over probe): active for X-Jpkpf-Reject: server-… with X-Jpkpf-Rule equal to the current hash, stale with another or no hash, missing when PHP's own reject header (no server-) answered, unknown for an answer without the header - OpenLiteSpeed cannot send one with its reject, and a proxy may remove it - unreachable for a transport error, 401, 403, 429, 5xx or a redirect, none when the settings produce no reject pattern.

stricter (the at_cap probe, a URL the plugin serves): true only on proof - the server rejected it with server-…. That is the red alarm. stricter_suspected: on LiteSpeed a 404/410 without header (OpenLiteSpeed rejects without one, but so does WordPress for a base it does not route), a hedged warning, never the alarm (ruling R19). stricter_checked: false when the at-cap probe did not get through (timeout, 401, 429 - the loopback sends no cookies, so a rate limit catches it -, 5xx, ...) or there was nothing to check; the detail then says why.

Keys robots, over, at_cap, each array{error: ?string, status: int, headers: array<string, string>, body: string} or null when not requested.

$inputs : array<string, mixed>

Rule inputs the probes were built from.

$server_software : string

SERVER_SOFTWARE of this site.

$robots_expected : bool = true

Does the plugin add lines to robots.txt on this site?

Tags
since

array{robots: string, rule: string, stricter: bool, stricter_checked: bool, stricter_suspected: bool, detail: string}

jpkcom_postfilter_server_rules_is_looser(array<string, mixed> $old, array<string, mixed> $new) : bool

True when union( $old, $new ) differs from $old (spec 7: N higher or 0, a group or a position without taxonomy added, strict URLs off, another endpoint, fragment or base, a filtered verdict). Compared on the values that shape the rule, as sets where they are sets; the hash is ignored. A state without groups rejects nothing whatever strict says, so strict counts only with groups. The reject status is left out (ruling R20): 404 or 410 changes how a rejected URL is answered, not which URLs are rejected.

Inputs before the change.

Inputs after it.

jpkcom_postfilter_server_html_text()

Text for the reject body: HTML-escaped and inert in every config syntax

jpkcom_postfilter_server_html_text(string $text) : string

The body is pasted into nginx return '…' (variables $x, escapes \), ISPConfig's brace counter ({ }), Apache's quoted ErrorDocument (expressions %{…}) and the Caddy/Ferron strings. A translation must not be able to reach any of them, so these characters become entities, and control characters become a space (the body is one line).

Every non-ASCII character becomes a numeric entity as well: Apache sends a string ErrorDocument as text/html; charset=iso-8859-1 (measured on 2.4.69, VirtualHost and .htaccess), and that header wins over the meta tag - "verfügbar" rendered as "verfÃ¼gbar". Pure ASCII reads the same whatever charset a server announces.

conn = max(1, floor(3W/8)) at most 3/8 of the workers render cookie-less filter pages at once, the rest stay free for the site rate = max(1, round(0.4 conn/t)) requests/s site-wide: keeps those workers 40 % busy on average burst = 2 rate ip_per_minute = 30, ip_burst = 10 a visitor without cookie gets 11 quick clicks, then one every 2 s bot_rate = max(1, round(2 rate/3)), bot_burst = 20 search engines' own bucket retry_after = 10 s

Anchor (spec 6, research report 3 §3, production: 8 workers, 0.4 s): conn 3, 3 r/s burst 6, 30 r/min burst 10 per IP, search engines 2 r/s burst 20.

Reject: a server-level if ($request_uri ~ …) (raw URI, server rewrite phase, before any location) rewrites to an internal exact location, because add_header is not allowed in a server-level if. return <status> '<body>' sends the body itself, so no error_page (and none of ISPConfig's error documents) runs. Rejected requests therefore never reach the rate-limit location either.

Rate limit: maps and zones only work in the http context (root); the per-base location carries the limits and hands valid requests on with the usual WordPress try_files. 429, not 503: ISPConfig's "Own Error-Documents" replace 503 together with its headers.

ISPConfig (research report 3 §1-§3): no location / (its merge replaces a location it already has), no line starting with # (it strips them), no brace inside a directive line (it counts braces per line), and the template's own location = /robots.txt is extended with ##merge##.

jpkcom_postfilter_server_snippets_apache()

server-rules-render.php : 885

Apache snippets: VirtualHost reject, mod_qos cap, ModSecurity limits

jpkcom_postfilter_server_snippets_apache(array<string, mixed> $inputs, array<string, int> $limits) : array<int, array{id: string, title: string, context: string, code: string}>

mod_qos (research report 4 §3a): QS_EventRequestLimit is a real concurrency cap on cookie-less filter requests. Never QS_ClientEventLimitCount: measured, it bans the client IP for every URL, cookie users included.

mod_qos has no bucket of its own for search engines: exempting their User-Agent would let anyone who fakes one past the only concurrency cap, so they share it (spec 6).

ModSecurity (§3b): everything inside a <LocationMatch> over the filter prefixes (decoded path - fine for a rate limit), including SecRuleEngine On, so OWASP CRS is not switched to blocking for the rest of the site. Phase 2, because Apache maps a request to its Location only after phase 1 rules ran (post_read_request). Fixed-window counters. The window starts with the first request (expirevar only when the counter is created); research set expirevar on every hit, which re-arms it - steady traffic then never resets a site-wide counter, and a visitor clicking every few seconds is blocked for good. Every deny rule is chained to its own class (cookie- less visitor or search engine), so a counter another rule set keeps cannot trigger it.

The counters live in RESOURCE (key jpkpf_ip_<addr>) and USER (key jpkpf_site_<server name>, via setuid), not in IP and GLOBAL: OWASP CRS 3.3 opens ip as <addr>_<UA hash> and global as global in phase 1, and ModSecurity 2 ignores a later initcol of an open collection. Measured on Debian 13 (CRS 3.3.7, modsecurity.conf active): a new User-Agent per request walked past the per-IP limit, and one VirtualHost's site-wide counter answered 429 on another. Custom collection names are not addressable in ModSecurity 2 ("Unknown variable").

Parameters
$inputs : array<string, mixed>

Rule inputs.

$limits : array<string, int>

Normalised rate limits.

Tags
since
1.6.0
Return values
array<int, array{id: string, title: string, context: string, code: string}>

jpkcom_postfilter_server_snippets_caddy()

server-rules-render.php : 1142

Caddy snippet: one `route` with the rejects first, then `rate_limit`

jpkcom_postfilter_server_snippets_caddy(array<string, mixed> $inputs, array<string, int> $limits) : array<int, array{id: string, title: string, context: string, code: string}>

Research report 2 §2. path_regexp sees the decoded path, so the reject is a CEL expression on the raw path and query. Both the reject and the rate-limit scope read the ORIGINAL request ({http.request.orig_uri}, {http.request.orig_uri.path}): the Caddyfile sorts rewrite and try_files before route, so a site-level try_files would otherwise have rewritten {http.request.uri} and path to /index.php first and silently disabled both. The original path is not cleaned, which is why the scope allows leading slashes (scope_regex()).

The pattern sits in a double-quoted CEL string inside a Caddyfile backtick token: the backticks pass every byte through, CEL then reads \\ as one backslash - so each \ of the pattern is doubled (\\+). A root base renders as an empty alternative (?:|news/), which RE2 accepts.

route keeps the written order. Outside it caddy-ratelimit sorts itself before respond, and every rejected request then used up the budget of the cookie-less visitors (verified in research). Inside it the segments block comes first: its respond ends the route, so a URL over both caps gets the guard's reason. The reject carries no-store - a cached reject would outlive a later loosening (spec 5.3).

Rate limit (caddy-ratelimit, sliding window of events per window): per IP ip_burst in the time ip_per_minute needs for them, site-wide (key static) and search engines' own zone over 10 s. Any Cookie header exempts. The 429 page carries no-store but no X-Robots-Tag: a busy answer for a valid URL must not tell search engines to drop it.

Parameters
$inputs : array<string, mixed>

Rule inputs.

$limits : array<string, int>

Normalised rate limits.

Tags
since
1.6.0
Return values
array<int, array{id: string, title: string, context: string, code: string}>

jpkcom_postfilter_server_snippets_ferron3()

server-rules-render.php : 1272

Ferron 3 snippets: top-level `match` blocks and host-level `if` blocks

jpkcom_postfilter_server_snippets_ferron3(array<string, mixed> $inputs, array<string, int> $limits) : array<int, array{id: string, title: string, context: string, code: string}>

Research report 2 §3.1 (3.0.0-rc.10, .conf format). match goes at the top level, where every host can use it (rc.10 also takes it inside a host), if only inside a host, hence two blocks. The reject matches request.uri (raw; request.uri.path is decoded) in a raw string r"…", so the pattern goes in unchanged; a root base's empty alternative (?:|news/) is valid in Rust's regex since 1.8. The if is decided once on the original URI, before any rewrite stage. The per-group matcher excludes the segments pattern, so a URL over both caps gets one status and the guard's reason.

Rate limit: rate_limit is a token bucket with an integer rate per second (1 is the smallest), per IP. Ferron has no constant key, so there is neither a site-wide rate nor a bucket of their own for search engines. Instead a FastCGI bulkhead: a second fcgi_php with its own connection pool, keyed by the URL string - it must differ from the main URL - and limit connections; further requests wait. The plugin does not know the backend URL: <php-backend-url> is a placeholder. A Unix socket cannot take the /jpkpf suffix (Ferron connects to the URL's whole path, so every request failed with 500 in the lab); a second spelling of the same path (/./) is the separate pool there.

Parameters
$inputs : array<string, mixed>

Rule inputs.

$limits : array<string, int>

Normalised rate limits.

Tags
since
1.6.0
Return values
array<int, array{id: string, title: string, context: string, code: string}>

jpkcom_postfilter_server_reject_patterns()

server-rules.php : 298

The two patterns a server may reject a filter URL on

jpkcom_postfilter_server_reject_patterns(array<string, mixed> $inputs[, string $subject = 'uri' ]) : array{per_group: ?string, segments: ?string}

Regexes without delimiters, for the raw request URI (path plus optional query). With B = the bases without their leading /, E = endpoint, N = terms per group, G = filter groups:

per_group: a segment below {B}{E}/ with N+1 or more non-empty pieces separated by literal + segments: segment G+1 contains a +, or there are G+4 segments

Why that is never stricter than the plugin, for a path without %:

  • urldecode() changes nothing but + there, and no rewrite rule literal contains +, so WordPress captures from the raw path.
  • The capture is the path after {E}/ minus an optional page/N / fragment suffix - at most three segments, none with a +. A segment with a + is therefore always part of the capture, and of G+4 segments at least G+1 are.
  • The guard rejects more than G non-empty segments (segments), and since 1.6.0 more than N non-empty raw pieces per taxonomy, counted before sanitize_title() and de-duplication (per-group). A literal + always separates pieces; %2b joining does not apply without %. Pieces of one taxonomy add up across segments, so one segment over the cap is enough.
  • A position whose group has no taxonomy is not counted by the guard, so per_group then only looks at the other positions - or at a position past G, which is a segments reject anyway.
  • per_group looks for the over-cap segment up to position G+3 only (bounded repetition, no JIT stack per segment); past that, and without %, segments matches anyway - with %, nothing does.

Both null when strict URLs are off, the guard's verdict is filtered (code may decide per request), there are no groups, no bases or no endpoint, or one base lies below another base's endpoint (a URL could then be captured by either base's rules, positions shifted). per_group is also null when N is 0 (unlimited).

request_line builds the same grammar for Apache's and OpenLiteSpeed's %{THE_REQUEST}, "METHOD URI PROTOCOL": anchored ^[A-Z]+ ... (?:\s|$), every negated class also excludes whitespace and the query is (?:\?\S*)?. The whitespace matters - "HTTP/1.1" contains a /, so a class that may cross the space counts "jpkpf-fragment HTTP/" as one more segment, and /blog/filter/a/b/page/2/jpkpf-fragment would be rejected although the plugin serves it. A URI cannot contain whitespace in a request line, so on every real request both forms decide the same. This form is PCRE-only (\s, \S); only the URI form is for RE2/Rust.

Parameters
$inputs : array<string, mixed>

As returned by jpkcom_postfilter_server_rule_inputs().

$subject : string = 'uri'

uri (raw request URI, default) or request_line (THE_REQUEST).

Tags
since
1.6.0
Return values
array{per_group: ?string, segments: ?string}

jpkcom_postfilter_migrate_pin_per_group_cap()

settings.php : 627

Keep existing installations at 3 terms per group

jpkcom_postfilter_migrate_pin_per_group_cap() : bool

1.6.0 lowers the default of max_filters_per_group from 3 to 2, for new installations only. The effective value of a key that was never stored is the default, so an installation that never saved the key (or never saved the General page at all) would silently drop to 2. This pins 3 for those.

Runs only on the step from a version before 1.6.0: the rewrite version marker is older than 1.6.0, or - an installation from before the marker existed (1.2.0) - it is empty and the filter groups option exists. A fresh install has neither; once the marker says 1.6.0 or later this never writes again, so a fresh 1.6.0 install keeps its 2 on every later update. Call before jpkcom_postfilter_maybe_flush_rewrites() updates the marker.

Only the stored array plus the pinned key is written; keys that were never stored stay missing and keep reading their defaults (merging the defaults in would freeze constant-derived ones such as debug_mode or url_endpoint). The General sanitizer is detached for this one write: it filters enabled_post_types / auto_inject against the post types registered at that moment (a CPT of a plugin that loads later would be dropped for good) and reads missing checkbox keys as "none selected". The add_option_* / update_option_* actions still run and refresh the memo and cache file.

Tags
since
1.6.0
Return values
bool —

True when the pin was written.

Since 1.5.0 an unknown slug is redirected away, which would have silently dropped every term of the other languages from their URLs.

One query per taxonomy per cache lifetime; the transient is keyed by taxonomy, never by requested slugs, and flushed with the term caches.

The one authority on "does this slug exist" - the request guard, the robots decision and the Abilities API all ask it, so "unknown" means the same thing everywhere. (No hooks, which is why it lives here.)

jpkcom_postfilter_split_segment()

url-policy.php : 480

Split a path segment into its term slugs

jpkcom_postfilter_split_segment(string $segment[, callable|null $known_slugs = null ][, string $taxonomy = '' ]) : array<string|int, string>

%2B counts as the separator too. Some link rewriters and normalisers encode +, and WordPress passes the escape through to the query var unchanged; read as part of one slug it made the whole selection "unknown" and redirected it to the unfiltered archive.

Except where %2b is part of a real slug. WordPress does not create such slugs itself (sanitize_title( 'C++' ) is c), but one typed into the slug field or imported as c%2b%2b is kept verbatim. A part that is a known slug stays whole; an unknown one is split at %2b and adjacent pieces are joined back, longest first, wherever they form a known slug - so c%2b%2b%2Bzaeune (two slugs joined by an encoded +) reads as c%2b%2b and zaeune.

Parameters
$segment : string

One path segment.

$known_slugs : callable|null = null

fn( string $taxonomy ): ?string[]; null = always split.

$taxonomy : string = ''

Taxonomy of the segment's position.

Tags
since
1.5.0
Return values
array<string|int, string> —

Raw parts (not yet sanitised).

jpkcom_postfilter_validate_filter_path()

url-policy.php : 565

Classify a requested filter path

jpkcom_postfilter_validate_filter_path(string $path, array<string|int, string> $taxonomies[, callable|null $known_slugs = null ][, string $unknown_action = 'redirect' ]) : array{action: string, reason: string, filters: array, unknown: bool}

Decides between "reject" (the path can never be a valid selection on this site) and "ok" with the normalised selection it stands for. Whether an ok path has to be redirected is decided by the caller, by comparing the request against the URL built from filters - one comparison that covers order, duplicates, case, empty segments, page/1 and the trailing slash.

Order of checks:

  1. more segments than filter groups -> reject (segments)
  2. a slug longer than 200 characters -> reject (length)
  3. caps per group, group count, total terms -> reject (per-group, groups, total) (per-group counts the non-empty raw pieces, summed per taxonomy, before normalising; see the file header)
  4. unknown slugs, per $unknown_action: redirect: dropped (the caller then redirects to what is left) noindex: kept, flagged reject: reject (unknown)

Before 1.5.0 the parser silently ignored extra segments and truncated over-cap selections, and every such URL rendered with 200.

Parameters
$path : string

Filter path as captured by the rewrite rule.

$taxonomies : array<string|int, string>

Taxonomies in position order.

$known_slugs : callable|null = null

fn( string $taxonomy ): ?string[] - known slugs, null when the taxonomy is gone. Null callable = no existence check.

$unknown_action : string = 'redirect'

'redirect' | 'noindex' | 'reject'.

Tags
since
1.5.0
Return values
array{action: string, reason: string, filters: array, unknown: bool}

jpkcom_postfilter_has_unknown_terms()

url-routing.php : 463

Whether the active filters reference term slugs that do not exist

jpkcom_postfilter_has_unknown_terms() : bool

Term slugs from the URL are sanitised but never checked for existence, so /blog/filter/does-not-exist/ renders a perfectly valid page with zero results. Left alone, every made-up slug is therefore an indexable, self-canonicalising thin-content URL that anyone can generate and link.

Since 1.5.0 the request guard handles them before the main query (unknown_terms_action, default: redirect to the selection without the unknown slugs). This check remains for the noindex action, for strict URLs switched off, and for the robots/canonical decision.

Validation reuses the transient-cached per-taxonomy term list, so this costs no extra query on a warm cache and cannot itself be used to flood the cache: the cache key is the taxonomy, never the requested slugs.

Tags
since
1.1.7
Return values
bool —

True if at least one requested slug is unknown.
